title: Popular NetFlix tech support scam
description: John Matarese has the details so you don't waste your money.

asr.full_text: A hotline you call to fix your computer or laptop may be a fake. John Mattarese has the Consumer Warning, so you don't waste your money. Everyone knows what tech support is. It's the department that updates and can often fix issues with cell phones, computers, tablets and all sorts of other gadgets. But scammers know that too. And they're now impersonating tech support centers more and more. The newest way to lose money and your computer at the same time? BUT SCAMMERS KNOW THAT TOO, AND THEY'RE NOW IMPERSONATING TK SUPPORT CENTERS MORE AND MORE. THE NEWEST WAY TO LOSE MONEY...AND YOUR COMPUTER AT THE SAME TIME.. ANSWER A CALL OR EMAIL FROM SOMEONE CLAIMING TO BE FROM TECH SUPPORT ... THE NEWEST CLAIMS TO BE FROM NETFLIX... AN EMAIL MESSAGE.. SAYING YOUR ACCOUNT IS SUSPENDED, AND ASKING FOR YOU TO RE-ENTER YOUR CREDIT CARD.. ANOTHER COMPONENT CLAIMS TO BE FROM VERIZON WIRELESS... SENDING YOU A BOGUS VERIZON 54 WEBSITE ... AND THE MOSTCONSIDERED CALL TO CONCILIATE THINGS. A SELF LOG AT THE BUSH, JUST WELCOME YOUR INCIDED CARD. ANOTHER ONE CLAIMS TO BE VERIZON WIRELESS SENDING YOU TO A BOGUS VERIZON 54 WEB SITE. THE MOST COMMON , A PHONE CALL FROM SOMEONE CLAIMING TO BE A MICROSOFT TECHNICIAN. I WAS GULLIBABLE AND HE COULD SHOW ME WHERE THE VIRUSES WERE AND SO I LET HIM TAKE CONTROL OF THE MOUSE." So from the Doesn't That Stink file..why these scams are so effective..they know that millions of people have microsoft pcs.. horizon phones and netflix accounts... And their copies of webpages and logos are so effective it looks real which may have you saying..doesn't that stink? It's a triple threat, fall for it and you'll be out money, your credit card will be compromised, and your computer could end up filled with mail-ware. JOHN HATELL remember be very suspicious of your own property and personal belongings. If you just need your own personal identity, I have a great idea of where and where to buy your property, but we want to buy a house and we don't sell it and I'm trying to make sure no one wants to buy it. it's really great for me, but it's a THERE HAS BEEN A TREAT. IT'S A TRIPLE THREAT. FALL FOR IT. IT'S OUT MONEY. YOUR CREDIT CARD COMPROMISED. YOUR COMPUTER COULD ENDS UP FILLED WITH MAILWARE. Remember..be very suspicious of any call or email that claims to be from company you do business with. Whether it's your bank, Verizon, Netflix, Microsoft, even Apple. Tell them you will do homework and you want to call them back before you divulge any information. And that way you don't waste your money. I'm John Madariz. ALL OF THIS IN HUNTERS

textual.observation: The source describes an email claiming an account is suspended and asking the recipient to re-enter credit-card information.

evidence.quote: AN EMAIL MESSAGE.. SAYING YOUR ACCOUNT IS SUSPENDED, AND ASKING FOR YOU TO RE-ENTER YOUR CREDIT CARD..

textual.context: Presented within a consumer-warning discussion of messages claiming to come from Netflix; the source does not establish whether a particular message was received or acted upon.
textual.potential_relevance: A claimed service identity and account-suspension condition are linked to a request to re-enter credit-card information, creating a concrete identity, urgency and sensitive-data relationship for later review.
textual.limitations: The records do not provide the sender, destination, whether the message was authentic, or whether anyone submitted information.

textual.observation: The source describes a communication claiming to be from Verizon Wireless that sends the audience to a site called bogus in the narration.

evidence.quote: ANOTHER COMPONENT CLAIMS TO BE FROM VERIZON WIRELESS... SENDING YOU A BOGUS VERIZON 54 WEBSITE ...

textual.context: Presented as an example in a consumer-warning report about impersonated tech-support-related communications; the wording is partially unclear and includes ASR errors.
textual.potential_relevance: A claimed Verizon Wireless affiliation is linked to directing the audience to a named website that the source characterizes as bogus, making the identity-and-destination relationship relevant for later assessment.
textual.limitations: The records do not provide the actual URL, show the website, or independently establish its ownership, authenticity or outcome.

textual.observation: The source recounts a phone call from someone claiming to be a Microsoft technician, followed by a demonstration of alleged viruses and permission for the caller to take control of the mouse.

evidence.quote: THE MOST COMMON , A PHONE CALL FROM SOMEONE CLAIMING TO BE A MICROSOFT TECHNICIAN. I WAS GULLIBABLE AND HE COULD SHOW ME WHERE THE VIRUSES WERE AND SO I LET HIM TAKE CONTROL OF THE MOUSE.

textual.context: Presented as a first-person illustrative account within a consumer-warning segment; the record does not establish whether the account is a reenactment, quotation or independently verified event.
textual.potential_relevance: A claimed Microsoft technician identity is linked to an alleged device problem and a request or permission for remote computer control, a concretely described mechanism requiring later context assessment.
textual.limitations: The records do not establish the caller's identity, whether the device contained viruses, what access was obtained, or what happened afterward.

visual.limitations: The sampled frames do not show the full spoken explanation, any actual call or email being received, or whether any specific entity contacted the viewer.

visual.observation: A red on-screen notice states that unusual activity was detected, the username was temporarily suspended, and to regain access the user should contact Member Services at a displayed 1-800 number.
visual.context: The notice is shown within the same visible news warning segment labeled "BEWARE TECH SUPPORT SCAMS" and "MAY CALL OR SEND YOU AN EMAIL."
visual.potential_relevance: The notice links an account-access problem and suspension claim to a requested phone contact with purported "Member Services," matching a concrete support/contact mechanism being discussed in a warning context.
visual.limitations: The frame does not establish who created the notice, whether the phone number is active, whether it was received by a real user, or whether the notice is authentic or deceptive.

visual.observation: A Netflix logo is shown on a screen while the lower-third still reads "BEWARE TECH SUPPORT SCAMS" and "MAY CALL OR SEND YOU AN EMAIL."
visual.context: The brand image appears during the same warning/news segment; no separate on-screen instruction is visible in this frame.
visual.potential_relevance: A recognizable service brand is visually associated with the segment’s warning about tech-support-related scam contacts, which may be relevant if the report is discussing branded account or support contact scenarios.
visual.limitations: The frame alone does not show any request to contact, pay, submit information, or visit a destination connected to Netflix, and it does not establish impersonation or misuse of the brand.

annotation.contextual_rationale: This video is non-scam content because it is presented as a local television consumer-protection report warning viewers about tech-support scams, not as an offer of support services or a request for participation. The examples of account-suspension messages requesting card information and callers claiming to be Microsoft technicians are presented as warning signs to recognize and avoid. Viewers are advised to distrust such calls or emails and independently contact companies before sharing information, while the Netflix imagery appears within that warning context without a separate offer.
annotation.fine_grained_rationale: The primary subject is a news-style warning that examines reported tech-support scam mechanisms, including impersonated support contacts, account-suspension messages, requests for credit-card information, and remote computer control. The segment gives cautionary advice rather than soliciting participation in those mechanisms.
